script.title: Why Mendeleev Left Gaps in His Table

lines: A Russian chemist drew up a table of the elements, with gaps in it.
His name was Dmitri Mendeleev, and the year was 1869.
Not all elements were known yet.
So there were gaps in his periodic table.
Mendeleev tied the chemical properties of elements to their atomic mass, a measure of an atom's weight.
Elements with similar chemical properties generally fell into the same group, or column.
You see, it's like a jigsaw puzzle with one piece missing.
The pieces around the hole show you its shape.
Mendeleev's periodic law said chemical properties depend on atomic mass.
If you know the elements around a missing one, it is easy to predict its properties.
So Mendeleev made bold predictions about elements no one had discovered.
He successfully predicted some properties of some of the missing elements.
His table became the first periodic table to be generally accepted.
In the late 19th century, his law was recognized as a fundamental discovery.
But the law was explained early in the 20th century, with atomic numbers and quantum mechanics.
Today, 118 elements are known, listed in order of increasing atomic number.
And 24 of them exist only when people make them in laboratories.

claims.claim: The first periodic table to become generally accepted was that of the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869; he formulated the periodic law as a dependence of chemical properties on atomic mass.
As not all elements were then known, there were gaps in his periodic table, and Mendeleev successfully used the periodic law to predict some properties of some of the missing elements.

Elements with similar chemical properties generally fall into the same group; it is relatively easy to predict the chemical properties of an element if one knows the properties of the elements around it.
Mendeleev made bold predictions about the chemical and physical properties of the undiscovered elements.

The periodic law was recognized as a fundamental discovery in the late 19th century. It was explained early in the 20th century, with the discovery of atomic numbers and associated pioneering work in quantum mechanics.
The periodic law states that when the elements are arranged in order of their atomic numbers an approximate recurrence of their properties is evident.
Today, 118 elements are known; the first 94 occur naturally on Earth and the remaining 24 occur only when synthesized in laboratories.

cast.mendeleev: a 35 year old Russian chemist, broad shouldered, a long untamed mane of light brown hair to his shoulders, a full bushy light brown beard, piercing pale blue eyes, wearing a dark grey wool frock coat over a black waistcoat and a loose white shirt, 1860s
cast.physicist: a 40 year old European physicist, slim, a smooth pale face, neat black hair parted in the middle, a black waxed handlebar moustache, wearing a dark navy three-piece suit with a gold watch chain and a white winged collar, 1910s
cast.scientist: a 30 year old Japanese laboratory scientist, a calm round face, a short black bob haircut, clear safety goggles, wearing a white lab coat over a lavender shirt and blue nitrile gloves, 2010s
